reason: The sources thoroughly corroborate the full technical story of the flag assembly, its jammed deployment, and its subsequent fate across multiple independent sites.
story: When Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, skeptics immediately questioned why the American flag appeared to wave in an airless environment. The explanation was purely mechanical. Because the Moon has no atmosphere, an ordinary flag would hang limp against its staff. Less than three months before launch, NASA engineer Jack Kinzler modified a standard five-dollar-and-fifty-cent nylon flag by sewing a hem along the top and inserting a telescoping horizontal rod to keep it visible. On the lunar surface, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin struggled to extend the rod completely in their bulky spacesuits. The jammed crossbar left the fabric bunched up, and along with tight packing creases, produced the permanent optical illusion of a waving banner. The flag never lasted long on its feet: during lunar liftoff, engine exhaust blew the assembly straight into the lunar dust.
angle: The American flag's famous lunar 'wave' wasn't wind or a hoax, but a five-dollar nylon flag held out by a telescoping curtain rod that jammed halfway during deployment.

claims.claim: Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin planted the first United States flag on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
Because the Moon has no atmosphere or wind, an ordinary flag would hang limp against its pole.
NASA added a horizontal rod across the top of the flag assembly so the flag would stay extended and visible without wind.
NASA engineer Jack Kinzler was tasked with designing the flag deployment mechanism less than three months before the Apollo 11 flight.
The Apollo 11 flag was a standard off-the-shelf nylon flag measuring 3 by 5 feet.
The standard nylon flag purchased for the mission cost $5.50.
The only modification made to the flag fabric was sewing a hem along its top edge to receive the horizontal support rod.
The flagpole tubing was constructed of gold-anodized aluminum tubes.
The entire Lunar Flag Assembly package weighed 9 pounds 7 ounces (4.3 kilograms).
The flag was enclosed in a protective stainless steel container to survive extreme exhaust temperatures from the descent engine.
The flag assembly was mounted on the ladder / forward landing leg of the Lunar Module.
Astronauts had difficulty fully extending the telescoping horizontal rod, which bunched up the fabric and left permanent ripple-like wrinkles.
Tight folding and packing of the flag during transit produced sharp creases that enhanced the illusion of waving.
Buzz Aldrin reported seeing the Apollo 11 flag get blown over by the Lunar Module's engine exhaust during liftoff.
Because the Apollo 11 flag was blown over at liftoff, later Apollo missions planted their flags farther from the Lunar Module.
Apollo missions planted a total of six American flags on the Moon.
Photographs from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter confirmed the flags deployed during Apollo 12, 16, and 17 were still standing decades later.
The flag planting was strictly symbolic and did not represent a territorial claim, in accordance with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.

disputed: Original flag manufacturer: NASA and popular sources cite Annin & Co., but a NASA contractor report notes that tags and bindings were stripped, creating uncertainty. Handle by omitting the manufacturer name or attributing as 'widely attributed to Annin & Co.'

Current state of flag fabric: While orbital shadows show flagpoles standing for Apollo 12, 16, and 17, vexillologist Annie Platoff and other experts debate whether solar radiation bleached the nylon white or disintegrated it into tatters. Handle by attributing: 'Experts theorize solar radiation may have bleached or disintegrated the nylon fabric.'
